sections.heading: Let the truth actually change me
sections.text: Lord, please do not let me miss the truth you have made known in the gospel. And do not let me be satisfied with having correct beliefs on paper if those beliefs are not leading me to Christ, turning me away from sin, and teaching me to live with self-control, integrity, and devotion to you. I do not want a faith that is only accurate in my head. I want the truth to save me, train me, and reshape the way I actually live.
theological_themes: The gospel is not merely a doctrinal system to admire but saving truth that produces holiness.
True knowledge of God leads to repentance, self-control, righteousness, and godliness in ordinary life.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes grace as something that not only brings salvation but also trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives. This directly grounds the prayer’s concern that doctrine must bear the fruit of real holiness.
This passage speaks of God’s desire for people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. It supports the prayer’s longing not to miss the saving truth of the gospel.

sections.heading: Do not let me lean on myself
sections.text: Keep me from trusting my own spiritual seriousness, my own convictions, or my own promises to do better. Those things are not strong enough to carry me. Make me strong in you, Lord, and in the strength you give. In every responsibility, every trial, and every fight against sin, teach me again that your grace is enough for me.
theological_themes: Human resolve is weak and cannot replace dependence on God.
God supplies strength and sufficient grace for duty, suffering, and spiritual conflict.

scripture_references.connection: Paul tells believers to be strong in the Lord and to stand in God’s armor, not in their own resources. This fits the prayer’s refusal to rely on personal resolve in spiritual conflict.
God’s answer to Paul’s weakness is the sufficiency of Christ’s grace and power. This supports the prayer’s confidence that grace is enough in trials and limitations.

sections.heading: Send me back to Christ in every trouble
sections.text: When I am spiritually distressed, when outward troubles press on me, and when the things I thought would satisfy me leave me empty, bring me back to you. Do not let me wander around looking for life where it cannot be found. Draw me to Jesus, full of grace and truth, the friend who does not turn away, the Savior who knows my weakness from the inside and is able to do far more for me than I know how to ask.
theological_themes: Creature comforts cannot finally satisfy the soul.
Christ is compassionate, sufficient, and able to help in weakness and trouble.
Believers are invited to come to God through Christ with confidence in distress.

scripture_references.connection: John presents Jesus as the Word made flesh, full of grace and truth, from whose fullness believers receive grace. This supports the prayer’s turning to Christ as the one who embodies and gives saving grace.

Hebrews teaches that Jesus sympathizes with human weakness and invites believers to draw near for mercy and help. This directly grounds the prayer’s movement toward Christ in spiritual distress and outward trouble.

Paul praises God as able to do abundantly beyond what believers ask or imagine. This supports the prayer’s confidence that Christ can provide more help than the praying person can fully understand or request.

sections.heading: Make my whole day belong to you
sections.text: Do not let my faith show up only in unusual moments, emergencies, or religious settings. Teach me to acknowledge you in all my ways. Do not let my devotion be limited to set times of prayer, as good and necessary as those are. Keep me living before you through the whole day—with reverence, trust, and obedience. Let me be yours not only when I gather with your people, but also at home, at work, in public, and in private.
theological_themes: Life with God is not confined to special occasions, places, or religious meetings.
The believer is called to acknowledge God and live before him in every ordinary part of life.

scripture_references.connection: This passage calls for trusting the Lord and acknowledging him in all one’s ways, not merely in religious moments. It supports the prayer’s desire for whole-life dependence and guidance.
Paul teaches that every word and deed should be done in the name of the Lord Jesus. This grounds the prayer’s concern that devotion reach home, public life, and ordinary daily actions.

sections.heading: Make godliness my life, not my costume
sections.text: Lord, do not let godliness become something I put on when it is useful or visible. Make it a settled pattern in me. More than a pattern, make it part of who I am in Christ. More than something I claim, make it the life I actually live by your Spirit. Use everything you appoint for me—your providence, your Word, worship, prayer, and praise—to do me real good. And when my earthly life is finished, bring me into the world where there is no temple because your glory fills everything, and the Lamb is its light.
theological_themes: True godliness is not performance but a Spirit-shaped life.
God uses providence and the means of grace to form believers.
The believer’s hope ends in the presence of God and the Lamb in the new creation.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to offer their bodies as living sacrifices and to be transformed rather than conformed to the world. This supports the prayer’s desire for godliness to become a whole-life reality rather than an outward display.

Peter teaches that God gives what is needed for life and godliness and makes believers partakers of the divine nature. This helps illuminate the prayer’s language about godliness becoming more than a habit—an inwardly transformed life.

John describes the new Jerusalem as having no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple and light. This directly supports the prayer’s final hope of entering the world filled with God’s glory and the Lamb.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase “means of grace” can carry different emphases across Christian traditions. I rendered it broadly as God using his Word, worship, prayer, praise, and providence to do spiritual good, without specifying a contested sacramental framework.

The original reference to being godly “on the sabbath or in thy house” reflects Puritan patterns of Lord’s Day observance and gathered worship. I preserved the substance—faith must extend beyond religious days and places—without turning the prayer into a detailed statement on Sabbath theology.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “a system of doctrine, however scriptural, that does not bring or further salvation” as a warning against resting in doctrinal correctness without saving union with Christ and practical holiness, not as a rejection of doctrine itself.
I rendered “creature comforts” as created things that can give real but limited comfort and cannot finally satisfy the soul.
I interpreted “dispensations” in its older sense of God’s providential dealings and circumstances, not in the modern theological sense of dispensationalism.

I kept the progression of “dress, habit, nature, life” by moving from outward performance, to settled pattern, to inward transformation, to lived reality, while avoiding language that would imply believers become divine by nature apart from grace.
